Empirical Research Plan: “Financial Constraints and Firms’ Real & Financial Policies in the 2008 Credit Crunch”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences (DID), complemented by a triple-difference and several robustness IV checks.

Rationale  
• The Lehman collapse (Sept-2008) triggered a virtually simultaneous, exogenous tightening of aggregate credit supply world-wide.  
• Firms differed ex-ante in how financially constrained they were.  
• By comparing the change in policies of “constrained” vs. “unconstrained” firms before vs. after the shock we can difference out any level differences between the two groups and any time shock common to all firms, isolating the causal interaction of the crisis with financial constraints.  
• Quarterly survey waves from 2007Q3–2008Q3 give us the “pre” period; the 2008Q4 wave is the “post”.  
• Because the shock was global but varied in intensity across regions, we will also estimate a triple-difference (DIDID): (constrained × post × U.S.) to exploit the fact that U.S. banks curtailed lending most sharply.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
FC_i ≡ 1 if firm i is ex-ante financially constrained.  Primary definition: the CFO answered “difficult” or “very difficult” to the question “How would you characterize your ability to raise bank credit today?” at 2008Q3 (the last pre-crisis wave).  

Alternative definitions for robustness  
a. No public debt rating.  
b. Bottom quartile of size within country × industry.  
c. Top quartile of pre-crisis cash-flow sensitivity of cash (CFSC) computed from Compustat history (public firms only).

Control group  
Firms that are not financially constrained under the same ex-ante metric (FC_i = 0).

Treatment timing  
Pre period: 2007Q3, 2007Q4, 2008Q1, 2008Q2, 2008Q3 surveys  
Post period: 2008Q4 survey (fielded Nov 25–Dec 5 2008 in the U.S.; similar dates elsewhere)

Running variable / cutoff  
Not applicable (DID not RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the credit-supply shock, the average change in investment, employment, etc. would have been the same for constrained and unconstrained firms.  Plausibility: We can test by plotting pre-crisis trends over five quarters; macro conditions were gradually deteriorating but there was no evidence that constrained firms were diverging before Lehman.

A2. Exogeneity of the shock: The timing and severity of the Lehman-driven crunch are unrelated to individual firms’ latent investment plans. Given the systemic nature of the shock, this is highly plausible.

A3. Stable composition: No massive entry/exit or survey-response changes differentially affecting one group exactly at Lehman. Plausible—the survey panel is stable; we will verify balanced-panel results.

A4. No spillovers that differentially benefit the control group (e.g., constrained firms dumping assets to unconstrained firms). Asset-sale regressions will help evaluate this risk.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Simultaneity / reporting bias: CFOs that already decided to slash investment might label themselves “credit-constrained.”  
Remedy: Base FC_i on answers from the last pre-Lehman wave (2008Q3) or on objective ex-ante characteristics (rating, size). We will also IV the post-Lehman self-reported constraint with the pre-Lehman dummy.

T2. Differential industry cyclicality: Some constrained firms cluster in more cyclical industries (e.g., durables), violating parallel trends.  
Remedy: Include industry × time fixed effects and interact pre-period industry growth rates with post dummy to soak up industry-specific demand shocks.

T3. Survey selection: If constrained firms were more likely to reply in 2008Q4, composition changes could bias results.  
Remedy: Use survey weights based on historical response propensities; replicate results in the public-firm Compustat sample using financial-statement outcomes for 2008–2009.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#---------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#---------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast lfe / did regressions
library(readr)
library(lmtest)      # coeftest, waldtest
library(sandwich)    # vcovHC
#---------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#---------------------------------------------------
survey_pre  <- fread("survey_2007Q3_2008Q3.csv")  # stacked pre quarters
survey_post <- fread("survey_2008Q4.csv")

# Harmonise variable names
setnames(survey_pre, tolower(names(survey_pre)))
setnames(survey_post, tolower(names(survey_post)))

survey_pre[, post := 0]
survey_post[, post := 1]

# Bind
surv <- rbindlist(list(survey_pre, survey_post), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

#---------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#---------------------------------------------------
# Ex-ante treatment: difficulty accessing credit in 2008Q3
fc_flag <- surv[quarter=="2008Q3", .(firm_id, hard_credit = (credit_difficulty %in% c("difficult","very_difficult")))]
surv <- merge(surv, fc_flag, by = "firm_id", all.x = TRUE)

# For nonrespondents in 2008Q3, fall back on rating
surv[is.na(hard_credit), hard_credit := (is.na(public_debt_rating))]

# Outcomes (planned % change for 2009 in the post wave;
# actual % change plans for 2008 in the pre waves)
numeric_outcomes <- c("capex_growth_plan", "employment_growth_plan",
                      "tech_spend_growth_plan", "marketing_growth_plan",
                      "cash_holdings_growth_plan", "dividend_growth_plan")

#---------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID regression (example: capex)
#---------------------------------------------------
did_capex <- feols(capex_growth_plan ~ post*hard_credit + firm_size + profitability +
                   i(industry, post) | firm_id + quarter,
                   data = surv, cluster = ~firm_id)

summary(did_capex)

#---------------------------------------------------
# 4. Triple Difference: U.S. vs non-U.S.
#---------------------------------------------------
did3_capex <- feols(capex_growth_plan ~ post*hard_credit*us_dummy +
                    firm_size + profitability |
                    firm_id + quarter + industry#post,
                    data = surv, cluster = ~firm_id)

#---------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: event-study style leads/lags
#---------------------------------------------------
# Keep balanced panel around shock
balanced <- surv[firm_id %in% surv[ , .N, by = firm_id][N == 6]$firm_id]

event_capex <- feols(capex_growth_plan ~ i(relative_quarter, hard_credit, ref= -1) +
                     firm_size + profitability |
                     firm_id + industry#quarter,
                     data = balanced, cluster = ~firm_id)

iplot(event_capex, xlab = "Quarters relative to Lehman", main = "CAPEX diff-in-diff event study")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that financially constrained firms will react more sharply to the external-finance shock:

• Capital expenditure: ≈10–15 pp lower planned 2009 growth than unconstrained firms.  
• Employment: ≈5–8 pp lower.  
• Cash holdings: Differential increase of ≈3–4 pp of assets (precautionary).  
• Credit-line drawdowns: ≈6–8 pp higher (LoC/Assets).  
• Dividends: Larger cut or cancellation probability (+15 pp).  
• Asset sales and project cancellation: materially higher incidence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-trend equality documented                                      1  
C2: Shock exogeneity & sharp timing                                    1  
C3: No sample composition change (checked with weights & balance)      0.5  
C4: No spillovers / interference                                       0.5  
C5: Robustness across alternative FC definitions / samples             1  
TOTAL = 4/5

With thorough pre-trend charts, alternative constraint definitions, industry-time controls, and IV robustness, the design should yield credible causal estimates of how financing frictions amplified the real effects of the 2008 credit crunch.
